newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's Schmidt rips Bundesbank on euro stance.
newsitem.headline: Germany's Schmidt rips Bundesbank on euro stance.

text.p: Former German Chancellor Helmut Schmidt blasted the Bundesbank for what he called its nefarious campaign against the euro and warned against delaying the single European currency because that could be tantamount to its ruin.

Schmidt, in an article in the weekly newspaper Die Zeit, wrote that a mere public discussion about delaying the euro would cause massive turbulence on currency markets and lead to higher unemployment throughout Europe.

Predicting a strong rise in the value of the mark and a sharp drop in value for the French franc, Italian lira and Spanish peseta if the euro were delayed, Schmidt said it was vital for the future of Europe that the single currency be launched on time in 1999.

"The members of the central bank council have been feeding the fears of an alleged instability of the euro for years," Schmidt said. "If these negative forces succeed, we will have to reckon with the worst consequences."

Schmidt, who as co-publisher of the newspaper has taken aim at the German central bank in the past for its position on the euro, complained that the media and politicians were not paying enough attention to the potential damage of a delayed or scrapped single currency.

"Can or should the euro be delayed? The debate is now hitting full stride," Schmidt said. "But we learn almost nothing from the politicians or the media about the serious problems that would result from the delay or failure of the euro."

Calling Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer Germany's "secret foreign minister," Schmidt said it was appalling the way the central bank had been demanding fiscal virtue from European partners while Germany itself was fudging its deficits to meet the single currency requirements.

"With its insistence of strict adherence to the Maastricht convergence criteria and its 'currency racism' against southern European countries and especially Italy, Germany has made itself more unloved than any time in the last 50 years," Schmidt wrote.
